label: Steps a day
body:
Heart and longevity benefits climb
steeply up to about 8,000 steps.
No gym needed. A 10-min walk after
meals also blunts sugar spikes.
caption:
You don't need 10,000 steps. But you probably need more than you're doing.

The 10k number came from a 1960s pedometer ad — not science.

What large studies actually show: the risk of early death drops steeply as daily steps rise, and the benefit starts levelling off around 7,000–8,000 steps for most adults.

Easy ways to get there:
→ 10-minute walk after each meal
→ Take calls standing or walking
→ Stairs instead of the lift
→ Park or get off one stop early

Walking is the most underrated health habit there is.

label: Nutrition
headline:
Vitamin D
in India
body: Most Indians are deficient despite the sun. Signs: fatigue, body aches, weak bones. Get 15–20 min of midday sun on arms and legs, and get tested.
caption:
India gets more sunshine than most countries. So why are most Indians low on vitamin D?

Indoor jobs, covered clothing, pollution and darker skin all cut how much your skin makes.

What low vitamin D can feel like:
→ Constant tiredness
→ Aching bones and muscles
→ Low mood
→ Getting sick often

What helps:
→ 15–20 min of midday sun on arms and legs, a few times a week
→ Eggs, fatty fish, fortified milk
→ A simple blood test — and a supplement only if your doctor says so

Don't guess. Test.

label: Myth buster
headline:
Fruit juice is
healthy?
body: Packaged juice has nearly as much sugar as a cola, and almost none of the fibre. Eat the whole fruit — it keeps you full and your blood sugar steady.
caption:
That "100% natural" juice box isn't the health drink it looks like.

Juicing strips out the fibre — the part that slows sugar down.

One 250 ml glass of packaged juice has roughly 20–25 g of sugar. A can of cola has about 27 g.

What happens without the fibre:
→ Sugar hits your blood fast
→ You're hungry again soon
→ It's easy to drink 3 oranges' worth in 30 seconds

The swap: eat the whole fruit. Same vitamins, plus fibre, plus actually feeling full.

label: Caffeine cutoff
body:
Caffeine has a ~5 hour half-life.
A 5 PM chai is still working
at 10 PM, cutting deep sleep.
Keep tea & coffee before 2 PM.
caption:
Sleeping badly even though you're exhausted? Check when you had your last chai.

Caffeine has a half-life of about 5 hours.

That means half the caffeine from a 5 PM coffee is still in your system at 10 PM — and some of it is still there at midnight.

Even if you fall asleep fine, late caffeine:
→ Reduces deep sleep
→ Makes sleep lighter and more broken
→ Leaves you groggy the next morning
→ So you reach for more caffeine… and repeat

The fix: keep tea and coffee before 2 PM. Switch to herbal tea after.

label: Reality check
headline:
Veg diet covers
every nutrient?
body: B12 comes almost only from animal foods. Many Indian vegetarians run low — tingling hands, fatigue, brain fog. Get tested and supplement if needed.
caption:
A vegetarian diet can be incredibly healthy. But there's one nutrient it struggles with.

Vitamin B12.

B12 is found almost entirely in animal foods — meat, fish, eggs, and smaller amounts in milk and curd. Plants don't make it.

Signs your B12 might be low:
→ Constant tiredness and weakness
→ Tingling or numbness in hands and feet
→ Brain fog and poor memory
→ Pale skin, breathlessness

What to do:
→ Include milk, curd, paneer daily
→ Get a B12 blood test
→ Supplement if your doctor recommends it

label: Training
headline:
Start strength
training
body: Two full-body sessions of squats, push-ups, rows and lunges build muscle, protect joints and improve blood sugar. Start with bodyweight.
caption:
Strength training isn't just for bodybuilders. It's one of the best things you can do for long-term health.

And you need far less than you think.

WHO recommends muscle-strengthening work at least 2 days a week. That's it.

What it does for you:
→ Builds and keeps muscle as you age
→ Stronger bones and joints
→ Better blood sugar control
→ Higher resting metabolism

A simple start: squats, push-ups (wall or knee is fine), rows, lunges. 2–3 sets each, twice a week.

label: Did you know
headline:
Rest days
build muscle.
body: Muscle grows while you recover, not while you lift. Training the same muscle hard every day just piles up fatigue. Give it about 48 hours.
caption:
Training hard every single day and not seeing results? You might need less, not more.

Lifting creates tiny damage in your muscles. They grow back stronger while you rest — not during the workout.

Skip recovery and you get:
→ Stalled strength
→ Constant soreness
→ Poor sleep and low energy
→ Higher injury risk

The rule of thumb: about 48 hours before training the same muscle group hard again. Walking and stretching on rest days is great.

Recovery is part of the program.

label: Max salt per day
body:
WHO's limit: under 5 g — about 1 tsp.
Most Indians eat far more.
Pickles, papad, namkeen & sauces
are the hidden sources.
caption:
You probably eat way more salt than you think — and most of it isn't from the salt shaker.

WHO recommends less than 5 g of salt a day. That's about one teaspoon, in total.

Studies show average intake in India is well above that.

Where the hidden salt comes from:
→ Pickles and papad
→ Namkeen, chips and biscuits
→ Sauces, ketchup and instant noodles
→ Restaurant and packaged food

Why it matters: too much salt raises blood pressure — a major cause of heart attacks and strokes.

label: Nutrition
headline:
Fibre, the
forgotten one
body: Keeps you full, feeds your gut bacteria and steadies blood sugar. Easy wins: whole dal and chana, fruit with skin, veggies at every meal, oats.
caption:
Everyone talks about protein. Almost no one talks about fibre — and most people don't get nearly enough.

The target for adults: around 25–30 g a day.

Why it matters:
→ Keeps you full longer (helps with weight)
→ Steadies blood sugar after meals
→ Feeds the good bacteria in your gut
→ Helps lower cholesterol

Easy Indian sources:
→ Whole dal, rajma, chana
→ Fruit with the skin on (guava, apple, pear)
→ A vegetable with every meal
→ Oats, whole wheat roti, millets

label: Myth buster
headline:
Skipping meals
burns more fat?
body: Fat loss comes from your overall calorie balance, not missed meals. Skipping often leads to overeating later. Pick a meal pattern you can actually stick to.
caption:
Skipping lunch to "save calories" and then raiding the kitchen at 6 PM? You're not alone.

There's nothing magic about skipping meals.

Fat loss comes down to your overall calorie balance across days and weeks. Two meals or five — it works the same if the total is the same.

What skipping often does instead:
→ Big hunger later → overeating
→ Low energy and irritability
→ Cravings for fried and sugary food
→ Less protein across the day

The best eating pattern is the one you can stick to — with protein in every meal.

label: Active minutes a week
body:
WHO's minimum for adults:
150 min of moderate activity.
That's just 30 min, 5 days a week.
Brisk walking counts.
caption:
Think you need an hour at the gym every day to be healthy? You don't.

WHO's minimum for adults: 150 minutes of moderate activity a week.

That's 30 minutes, 5 days a week.

What counts as moderate (you can talk, but not sing):
→ Brisk walking
→ Cycling
→ Swimming
→ Dancing, sports, even vigorous housework

Add 2 days of strength training and you've hit the full recommendation.

Something is always better than nothing.

label: Reality check
headline:
Always tired?
It's just stress?
body: Not always. Low iron, B12, vitamin D or thyroid issues are common causes — especially in Indian women. A simple blood test can tell.
caption:
Tired all the time, even after sleeping? Don't just blame stress.

Ongoing fatigue often has a fixable cause.

Common ones worth checking:
→ Low iron / anaemia (very common in Indian women)
→ Low vitamin B12
→ Low vitamin D
→ Thyroid problems
→ Poor sleep quality

A basic blood panel — CBC, ferritin, B12, vitamin D, TSH — can rule most of these in or out.

If tiredness has lasted weeks, talk to a doctor. It's not "just how you are."

label: Sleep
headline:
Sleep better
tonight
body: Your body clock loves routine. Get morning sunlight, keep your room cool and dark, and put the phone away 30 minutes before bed.
caption:
Struggling to fall asleep — or waking up tired? The fix usually starts in the morning, not at night.

Your body clock runs on routine. The single most powerful habit: wake up at the same time every day, weekends included.

Then add:
→ 10 minutes of morning sunlight
→ No caffeine after 2 PM
→ A cool, dark, quiet room
→ Phone away 30 minutes before bed

Give it two weeks. Consistency beats any sleep gadget.

label: Did you know
headline:
Your resting
heart rate talks.
body: Normal is 60–100 bpm, and fitter people sit lower. If yours stays higher than usual for days, it can signal poor sleep, stress or illness.
caption:
Your resting heart rate is one of the simplest health signals you can track — and it's free.

Measure it in the morning, before getting out of bed.

What the numbers mean:
→ 60–100 bpm is the normal adult range
→ Regular exercise usually brings it lower over time
→ A rise of several beats for days can mean poor sleep, stress, dehydration or an oncoming illness

Track it for a week to learn your baseline. Changes matter more than one reading.

If it's often above 100 at rest, or you feel palpitations or dizziness, see a doctor.

label: Healthy blood pressure
body:
Below 120/80 mmHg is ideal.
140/90 or above on repeat checks
is high BP. It rarely has symptoms,
so the only way to know is to check.
caption:
High blood pressure is called the silent killer for a reason. Most people with it feel completely fine.

Until a heart attack or stroke.

What the numbers mean:
→ Below 120/80 — ideal
→ 120–139 / 80–89 — higher than ideal, time to act
→ 140/90 or above on repeat readings — high blood pressure

What brings it down:
→ Less salt (pickles, papad, namkeen, packaged food)
→ 150 minutes of activity a week
→ Losing even a few kg if you're overweight
→ Less alcohol, no smoking

Every adult should know their number. Get it checked at least once a year.

label: Wellbeing
headline:
Breathe out
the stress
body: Breathe in for 4 counts, out for 6. A longer exhale slows your heart rate and calms you down. Five minutes is enough.
caption:
Feeling wound up before a meeting, an exam or a tough conversation? Your breath is the fastest off-switch you have.

And it's free.

When you breathe out slowly, your heart rate drops a little and your body shifts out of "fight or flight".

Try it right now:
→ Breathe in through your nose for 4 counts
→ Breathe out slowly through your mouth for 6 counts
→ Keep your shoulders relaxed
→ Repeat for 5 minutes

Use it before sleep, in traffic, or whenever stress spikes.

Slow breath, calm mind.

label: Myth buster
headline:
Eating late
makes you fat?
body: A calorie at 10 PM counts the same as one at 1 PM. The real problem is mindless late-night snacking, and heavy dinners that disturb sleep.
caption:
"Don't eat after 7 PM or you'll gain weight." Heard this one?

Your body doesn't have a clock that turns food into fat after sunset.

Weight change comes from your total calories over days and weeks — not the time on the clock.

Why late eating gets the blame:
→ Late-night snacking is usually extra food, not a meal
→ It's often chips, sweets and biscuits
→ A heavy dinner right before bed can cause acidity and poor sleep
→ Poor sleep makes you hungrier the next day

The smart move: eat dinner 2–3 hours before bed and keep it balanced. If you're truly hungry later, curd, fruit or a handful of nuts.

label: Added sugar a day
body:
WHO's ideal limit: about 6 tsp.
3 cups of chai with 2 tsp each
already hits it — before any
sweets, biscuits or cold drinks.
caption:
How many teaspoons of sugar do you have a day? Most people have no idea.

WHO advises keeping added sugar below 10% of your daily calories — and ideally below 5%. For most adults, that's about 25 g, or 6 teaspoons.

Where it sneaks in:
→ Chai and coffee (2 tsp a cup adds up fast)
→ Biscuits, rusks and "healthy" cereals
→ Cold drinks and packaged juice
→ Ketchup, sauces and flavoured yoghurt

Easy cuts:
→ Reduce sugar in chai by half a spoon every week
→ Swap biscuits for fruit or nuts
→ Water or chaas instead of cold drinks

Your taste buds adjust within a few weeks.

label: Reality check
headline:
Multigrain means
healthy?
body: Many multigrain breads and biscuits are mostly maida with a sprinkle of other grains. Check the ingredients list — the first item is the main one.
caption:
"Multigrain" on the pack sounds healthy. But it doesn't mean whole grain.

It just means more than one grain is in there — even if it's a tiny amount.

Many multigrain breads, biscuits and atta blends are mostly refined flour (maida) with a little oats, ragi or flax added for the label.

How to check in 10 seconds:
→ Read the ingredients list — they're listed from most to least
→ First ingredient should be "whole wheat" or another whole grain
→ "Wheat flour" or "refined wheat flour" usually means maida
→ Compare fibre: aim for 6 g or more per 100 g

Trust the ingredients, not the front of the pack.

label: Training
headline:
Your first
push-up

sections.title: Week 3–4
sections.text: Hands on a table or bed edge.

sections.title: Week 5+
sections.text: Knees on the floor, then full.

caption:
Can't do a single push-up? Good news — almost everyone can get there in a few weeks.

The trick is making it easier first, then harder step by step.

The progression:
→ Wall push-ups: 3 sets of 10
→ Incline push-ups: hands on a table, kitchen counter or bed edge
→ Knee push-ups on the floor
→ Full push-ups

Move to the next level when you can do 3 clean sets of 10.

Form tips: body in a straight line, elbows at about 45° from your body, lower your chest, not your head.

Push-ups build chest, shoulders, arms and core — no equipment needed.

label: Did you know
headline:
Your ears clean
themselves.
body: Ear wax moves out on its own as you chew and talk. Cotton buds push it deeper and can hurt your eardrum. Just wipe the outer ear.
caption:
Cleaning your ears with cotton buds every day? You're probably doing more harm than good.

Ear wax isn't dirt. It traps dust, keeps the ear canal moist and helps fight infection.

Your ears are self-cleaning: jaw movement slowly pushes old wax outwards.

What cotton buds actually do:
→ Push wax deeper, causing blockages
→ Scratch the delicate skin of the ear canal
→ Can damage your eardrum

What to do instead:
→ Wipe the outer ear with a cloth after a bath
→ Never put hairpins, keys or oil drops inside
→ See a doctor for pain, blocked hearing or discharge

Leave your ears alone. They've got this.

label: HbA1c warning line
body:
HbA1c shows your average sugar
over the last 2–3 months.
Below 5.7% normal. 5.7–6.4%
prediabetes. 6.5%+ diabetes.
caption:
A fasting sugar test shows one morning. HbA1c shows the last 2–3 months.

That's why doctors trust it.

HbA1c measures how much sugar has stuck to your red blood cells, which live about 3 months.

What the result means:
→ Below 5.7% — normal
→ 5.7% to 6.4% — prediabetes
→ 6.5% or higher — diabetes (confirmed by your doctor)

Prediabetes is the window where lifestyle changes work best:
→ Lose 5–7% of your body weight if overweight
→ 150 minutes of activity a week
→ Fewer refined carbs and sugary drinks

Over 30, or diabetes in the family? Ask for an HbA1c test.

label: Heart health
headline:
Heart attack
warning signs

sections.title: Chest
sections.text: Pressure, squeezing or pain lasting minutes.

sections.title: Spreading
sections.text: To the arm, jaw, neck or back.

caption:
Knowing these signs can save a life — maybe someone at home.

In a heart attack, every minute matters.

Common warning signs:
→ Chest pressure, squeezing or pain that lasts more than a few minutes
→ Pain spreading to the arm, jaw, neck, back or upper stomach
→ Shortness of breath
→ Cold sweat, nausea or light-headedness

Women, older people and people with diabetes often have milder or unusual symptoms — like only breathlessness, tiredness or "gas".

What to do:
→ Call 108 or 112 straight away
→ Don't drive yourself to hospital
→ Don't wait to "see if it passes"

Share this with your family.

label: Myth buster
headline:
Carbs make
you fat?
body: Extra calories make you gain fat — from any source. Dal, fruit, millets and whole grains are healthy carbs. Big portions of refined carbs are the problem.
caption:
Rice, roti and fruit aren't the enemy. Cutting all carbs isn't the secret to fat loss.

Weight gain comes from eating more calories than you use — whether they come from carbs, fat or protein.

Where carbs go wrong:
→ Huge portions of white rice or maida
→ Sugary drinks, sweets and biscuits
→ Fried snacks (carbs + oil = easy to overeat)
→ Carbs with almost no protein or vegetables

Where carbs are great:
→ Dal, rajma, chana
→ Fruit and vegetables
→ Millets, oats, whole wheat roti

The fix isn't zero carbs. It's better carbs, sensible portions, and protein on the plate.

label: Waist limit in cm
body:
For South Asians, risk rises above
90 cm waist for men, 80 cm for women.
It tracks belly fat around organs —
better than weight alone.
caption:
Your waist size may say more about your health than your weight does.

South Asians tend to store fat around the belly and organs (visceral fat) — even at a "normal" weight.

That fat is linked to diabetes, heart disease and fatty liver.

Risk rises above:
→ 90 cm (about 35.5 inches) for men
→ 80 cm (about 31.5 inches) for women

How to measure:
→ Stand straight and breathe out normally
→ Measure around your belly at the level of your navel
→ Tape snug, not pressing into the skin

Bringing it down: strength training, daily walking, more protein and fibre, less sugar and refined carbs.

label: Reality check
headline:
Sugar-free
sweets are safe?
body: Most are still made with khoa, ghee and refined flour. They can be just as high in calories, and many still raise blood sugar. Portion matters.
caption:
"Sugar-free" mithai is a festival favourite. But it isn't a free pass.

Sugar-free usually just means no table sugar was added.

What's often still inside:
→ Khoa and ghee — high in calories and saturated fat
→ Maida or other refined flour
→ Dried fruit and natural sugars
→ Sugar alcohols that can upset your stomach in large amounts

For people with diabetes, many sugar-free sweets still raise blood sugar.

Smarter ways to enjoy sweets:
→ Have a small piece, not a box
→ Eat it after a meal, not on an empty stomach
→ Share, and go for a walk after

Enjoy the festival. Just read beyond the label.

label: Gut health
headline:
Curd for
your gut
body: Homemade curd is rich in live cultures, protein and calcium. Have it plain, as raita or chaas. Skip the sugary flavoured versions.
caption:
One of the best foods for your gut is probably already in your fridge.

Curd (dahi).

Fermentation fills it with live bacteria — the friendly kind that support a healthy gut.

What a bowl of curd gives you:
→ Live cultures for gut health
→ Protein to keep you full
→ Calcium for bones
→ Easy digestion for many people who struggle with milk

Easy ways to have it:
→ Plain with lunch
→ Raita with vegetables
→ Chaas on hot afternoons
→ Hung curd as a dip

Skip flavoured, sweetened tubs — they can hold several teaspoons of sugar.

label: Did you know
headline:
Tea with meals
blocks iron.
body: Tannins in tea and coffee cut how much iron you absorb from food. Keep a one-hour gap. Pair dal or greens with lemon or amla instead.
caption:
Chai right after lunch is a habit for many of us. It may be costing you iron.

Tea and coffee contain tannins and polyphenols. They bind to the iron in plant foods and reduce how much your body absorbs.

This matters a lot in India, where anaemia is very common — especially in women.

Simple fixes:
→ Keep a gap of about an hour between meals and chai or coffee
→ Add vitamin C to iron-rich meals: lemon, amla, guava, tomato
→ Eat iron-rich foods: dal, chana, rajma, green leafy veg, ragi
→ Get your haemoglobin checked if you're always tired

Same chai, better timing.

label: Safe level of alcohol
body:
WHO: no amount of alcohol is safe
for health. Risk of cancer and
other harm starts from the first
drink and rises with every one.
caption:
"A drink a day is good for the heart." That idea hasn't held up.

In 2023, WHO stated that there is no safe level of alcohol consumption for health.

Alcohol is a Group 1 carcinogen — the same category as tobacco.

What alcohol is linked to:
→ At least 7 types of cancer, including breast and bowel
→ High blood pressure and heart rhythm problems
→ Fatty liver and liver disease
→ Poor sleep, weight gain and low mood

If you drink:
→ Less is always better
→ Have alcohol-free days every week
→ Never drink and drive

The healthiest amount is none.

label: Sleep
headline:
Can't sleep?
Get up.
body: Lying awake teaches your brain that bed means stress. Get up, sit somewhere dim and calm, and go back only when you're sleepy.
caption:
Tossing and turning for an hour? Staying in bed is making it worse.

When you lie awake night after night, your brain starts linking your bed with frustration, not sleep.

Sleep doctors use a simple rule:
→ If you're awake for about 20 minutes, get out of bed
→ Sit somewhere dim and quiet
→ Read a paper book or listen to something calm — no phone
→ Go back to bed only when you feel sleepy
→ Repeat if needed

Also: keep the same wake-up time, even after a bad night.

It feels strange at first, but it retrains your brain to fall asleep in bed.

label: Myth buster
headline:
Sweating more
burns more fat?
body: Sweat is how your body cools down, not how it burns fat. The weight you lose is water, and it comes back as soon as you drink.
caption:
Wearing a sweat suit or working out in a hot room to "melt the fat"? It doesn't work like that.

Sweat is water your body releases to cool down.

How much you sweat depends on heat, humidity, genetics and fitness — not on how much fat you're burning.

What really happens:
→ You lose water weight
→ The scale drops for a few hours
→ You drink water, and it comes right back
→ Too much sweating can leave you dehydrated and dizzy

What does burn fat: a consistent calorie deficit, strength training, daily movement and enough protein.

Judge your workout by effort and progress, not sweat.

label: BMI cutoff for Indians
body:
For Asian Indians, BMI 23–24.9
counts as overweight, 25+ as obese.
The global cutoffs (25/30) miss
risk that starts earlier for us.
caption:
Your BMI says "normal"? For Indians, the usual chart can be misleading.

Asian Indians tend to develop diabetes and heart disease at lower body weights than Western populations.

That's why Indian guidelines use lower cutoffs:
→ 18.5–22.9 — normal
→ 23–24.9 — overweight
→ 25 and above — obese

How to calculate: weight (kg) ÷ height (m) ÷ height (m).
At 1.70 m and 68 kg → BMI 23.5 → overweight by Indian cutoffs.

BMI is only a starting point. Check your waist size too — belly fat is the bigger warning sign.

label: Reality check
headline:
Protein bars are
health food?
body: Many protein bars carry as much sugar and calories as a chocolate bar. Check the label. A handful of nuts, chana or curd often does better.
caption:
That protein bar in your gym bag might be a chocolate bar in disguise.

Many popular bars contain:
→ 10–20 g of sugar or syrups
→ 200–300 calories
→ Less protein than the front of the pack suggests
→ Sugar alcohols that can cause bloating

Before you buy, check the label:
→ Protein should be at least 15 g per bar
→ Sugar ideally under 5 g
→ A short ingredients list you understand

Real-food swaps with protein:
→ Roasted chana
→ A bowl of curd or paneer
→ Boiled eggs
→ Sprouts chaat

A bar is fine in a pinch. It isn't a health food.

label: Women's health
headline:
Know your
cycle
body: Count from the first day of one period to the next. Bleeding usually lasts 2–7 days. Track it — changes are worth telling a doctor.
caption:
Your period is one of the best signals of your overall health. Do you know what's normal for you?

For adults, a normal cycle is 21 to 35 days, counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. Bleeding usually lasts 2 to 7 days.

See a doctor if:
→ Periods suddenly become irregular
→ You miss periods for 3 months or more (and aren't pregnant)
→ You soak through a pad every 1–2 hours
→ Pain stops you from daily activities
→ You bleed between periods

Track your cycle in a notes app or calendar. Patterns tell your doctor a lot.

label: Did you know
headline:
Your bones
are alive.
body: Bone is constantly broken down and rebuilt. You build most of your bone mass by your late 20s, so strength training and calcium matter early.
caption:
Bones aren't dead scaffolding. They're living tissue that rebuilds itself every day.

Your body is always breaking down old bone and laying down new bone.

Most people reach their peak bone mass by around age 30. After that, keeping it is the goal.

What builds strong bones:
→ Strength training and impact (walking, stairs, skipping)
→ Calcium: milk, curd, paneer, ragi, sesame
→ Vitamin D from sunlight (and testing if you're low)
→ Enough protein

What weakens them:
→ Smoking and heavy drinking
→ Very low body weight
→ Sitting all day

Build it young. Keep it for life.

label: Ideal power nap
body:
A 10–20 min nap boosts alertness
without the grogginess.
Longer naps drop you into deep sleep.
Nap before 3 PM to protect the night.
caption:
Afternoon slump? A short nap can work better than another cup of chai.

The sweet spot is 10–20 minutes.

Why short works best:
→ You stay in light sleep and wake up refreshed
→ Longer naps take you into deep sleep — waking from it leaves you groggy
→ Late or long naps make it harder to sleep at night

How to nap well:
→ Set an alarm for 20 minutes
→ Nap before 3 PM
→ Dim the lights, or use an eye mask
→ Even resting with your eyes closed helps

If you need long naps every day, check your night-time sleep first.

label: Nutrition
headline:
Read the
label

sections.title: Sugar
sections.text: Over 10 g per 100 g is a lot.

sections.title: Sodium
sections.text: Over 600 mg per 100 g is high.

caption:
The front of the pack is marketing. The back of the pack is the truth.

Ten seconds with a label can change what goes in your trolley.

What to look at:
→ Ingredients: listed from most to least. If sugar or maida comes first, that's the main thing you're eating
→ Serving size: brands often use tiny servings to make numbers look small
→ Always compare per 100 g between brands
→ Sugar: more than 10 g per 100 g is a lot for a snack
→ Sodium: more than 600 mg per 100 g is high
→ Trans fat: look for 0 g and no "partially hydrogenated oil"

Words like "natural", "lite" and "multigrain" don't mean healthy.

label: Myth buster
headline:
Lemon water
burns fat?
body: No drink melts fat. Lemon water is a fine, low-calorie swap for juice or cold drinks, but it doesn't speed up fat loss on its own.
caption:
Warm lemon water with honey on an empty stomach — the famous "fat cutter". Sadly, it doesn't cut fat.

There's no evidence that lemon, honey, jeera water or any other drink burns body fat.

What lemon water can do:
→ Help you drink more water
→ Replace sugary drinks (a real win)
→ Add a little vitamin C

What it can't do:
→ Burn belly fat
→ "Detox" your body
→ Make up for the rest of your diet

And the honey adds sugar and calories.

Fat loss still comes from eating a bit less, moving more, and sleeping well. Drink lemon water because you like it, not as a cure.

label: Fruit & veg daily
body:
WHO's minimum: about 5 portions.
One portion ≈ 80 g, roughly a
handful. Potatoes don't count.
Aim for different colours daily.
caption:
How many portions of fruit and vegetables did you eat yesterday? Most people fall short.

WHO recommends at least 400 g a day — about 5 portions of 80 g.

What one portion looks like:
→ 1 medium fruit (apple, banana, guava, orange)
→ A small bowl of sabzi
→ A bowl of salad
→ A handful of berries or grapes

Potatoes and other starchy roots don't count towards the 5.

Easy ways to get there:
→ Fruit with breakfast
→ Two sabzis at lunch, not one
→ Salad or cucumber with dinner
→ Fruit as your evening snack

More colours = more nutrients.

label: Reality check
headline:
5 hours of
sleep is fine?
body: Adults need 7 or more hours. People who sleep too little stop noticing how impaired they are, while focus, mood and blood sugar keep slipping.
caption:
"I'm fine on 5 hours." Many people say it. Very few actually are.

Adults need at least 7 hours of sleep a night.

In sleep studies, people kept on short sleep for two weeks performed worse and worse on attention tests — but felt only slightly sleepy. They got used to the feeling, not the damage.

Regular short sleep is linked to:
→ Weight gain and more cravings
→ Higher blood sugar and blood pressure
→ Poor focus, memory and mood
→ More colds and infections

Start small: go to bed 15 minutes earlier each week until you reach 7 hours.

You can't train your body to need less sleep.

label: Training
headline:
Squat the
right way

sections.title: Down
sections.text: Hips back, as low as is comfortable.

sections.title: Knees
sections.text: Track over your toes, not caving in.

caption:
The squat is the one exercise everyone should master. It's how you get up from a chair, the floor, or a car.

Do it well and it builds your legs, hips and core — and protects your knees.

Step by step:
→ Feet about shoulder-width apart, toes turned slightly out
→ Push your hips back like you're sitting on a chair
→ Keep your chest up and your back neutral
→ Let your knees follow your toes — don't let them cave in
→ Go as low as is comfortable, then stand up through your whole foot

Beginners: squat down to a chair and stand back up. 3 sets of 10.

Knees going past your toes is fine if it feels fine.

label: Did you know
headline:
Fullness takes
20 minutes.
body: Your gut takes around 20 minutes to tell your brain you're full. Eat fast and you overshoot. Slow down, chew well, and pause halfway.
caption:
Ever finished a meal, felt fine, and then 15 minutes later felt stuffed? That's the fullness delay.

It takes around 20 minutes for your gut's "I'm full" signals to reach your brain.

When you eat in 5 minutes, you can easily eat more than you need before that signal arrives.

How to slow down:
→ Put your spoon or roti down between bites
→ Chew each bite properly
→ Don't eat in front of a screen
→ Start with salad or a bowl of dal
→ Pause halfway and check how hungry you still are

Eating slowly is one of the easiest ways to eat less without trying.

label: Brush, twice a day
body:
Brush for 2 minutes, morning and
night, with fluoride toothpaste.
Spit, but don't rinse after —
let the fluoride keep working.
caption:
Most people brush for about 45 seconds. Dentists recommend 2 full minutes, twice a day.

Your mouth health is linked to your whole body, including your heart and blood sugar.

The basics:
→ 2 minutes, morning and before bed
→ Fluoride toothpaste, a pea-sized amount
→ Soft brush, small circles, gentle pressure
→ Spit out the toothpaste, but don't rinse with water straight after
→ Clean between teeth daily (floss or interdental brush)
→ Replace your brush every 3 months

Bleeding gums aren't normal — see a dentist.

Two minutes, twice a day. Use a song or a timer.

label: Heart health
headline:
Check BP
at home

sections.title: Before
sections.text: Rest 5 min. No chai or exercise for 30.

sections.title: Position
sections.text: Back supported, feet flat, arm at heart level.

sections.title: Readings
sections.text: Take 2, one minute apart. Note both.

caption:
A home BP machine is one of the most useful health gadgets you can own — if you use it right.

Wrong technique can throw readings off by 10 points or more.

How to measure properly:
→ No tea, coffee, smoking or exercise for 30 minutes before
→ Sit for 5 minutes with your back supported
→ Feet flat on the floor, legs uncrossed
→ Cuff on bare upper arm, at heart level
→ Don't talk during the reading
→ Take 2 readings, 1 minute apart

Measure at the same times — morning and evening — for a week, and show the log to your doctor.

One high reading isn't a diagnosis. A pattern is.

label: Myth buster
headline:
Eggs raise your
cholesterol?
body: For most healthy people, an egg a day has little effect on blood cholesterol. Fried sides, trans fats and saturated fats matter far more.
caption:
Eggs were blamed for high cholesterol for decades. The science has moved on.

For most healthy people, the cholesterol you eat has a fairly small effect on the cholesterol in your blood.

Large studies have found that up to one egg a day isn't linked to higher heart disease risk in most people.

What raises blood cholesterol more:
→ Trans fats (vanaspati, some fried snacks, bakery items)
→ Lots of saturated fat
→ Excess weight and inactivity

Eggs give you:
→ About 6 g of high-quality protein each
→ Vitamin B12, vitamin D and choline

If you have diabetes or high LDL, ask your doctor what's right for you.

label: Lower diabetes risk
body:
In a large US trial, losing ~7%
body weight and 150 min/week of
activity cut diabetes risk by 58%
in people with prediabetes.
caption:
Prediabetes doesn't have to become diabetes.

The landmark Diabetes Prevention Program followed over 3,000 adults with prediabetes.

The lifestyle group aimed for:
→ About 7% weight loss
→ 150 minutes of activity a week (mostly brisk walking)

Result: they were 58% less likely to develop type 2 diabetes over about 3 years — better than the medicine group.

What that looks like at 80 kg → losing about 5–6 kg.

Small changes that add up:
→ Walk after meals
→ Smaller portions of rice and roti
→ More dal, vegetables and protein
→ Swap sugary drinks for water or chaas

Your habits are powerful medicine.

label: Reality check
headline:
Detox teas
cleanse you?
body: Your liver and kidneys already detox you, 24/7. Many detox teas contain laxatives — the weight you lose is water and stool, not fat.
caption:
Detox teas promise a flat stomach in 14 days. Here's what they actually do.

Your body already has a full-time detox system: your liver, kidneys, gut, lungs and skin.

Many "detox" or "slimming" teas contain senna or other laxatives.

What that means:
→ Frequent trips to the toilet
→ Water loss, so the scale drops briefly
→ Cramps, bloating and dehydration
→ Long-term use can upset your gut and electrolytes

What genuinely supports your liver and kidneys:
→ Enough water
→ Less alcohol
→ Fibre-rich food
→ Sleep and exercise

Save your money. Your organs have this covered.

label: Mental health
headline:
5-4-3-2-1
grounding
body: Anxious? Name 5 things you see, 4 you touch, 3 you hear, 2 you smell, 1 you taste. It pulls you back to now.
caption:
When anxiety hits, your mind races ahead to everything that could go wrong. This simple trick brings it back.

It's called 5-4-3-2-1 grounding.

Notice and name:
→ 5 things you can see
→ 4 things you can touch
→ 3 things you can hear
→ 2 things you can smell
→ 1 thing you can taste

Say them out loud or in your head. Take your time.

It works by shifting your attention from anxious thoughts to your senses, right here, right now.

Use it before a presentation, during a panic, or at 2 AM.

If anxiety is affecting your daily life, talking to a professional helps.

label: Did you know
headline:
Outdoor time
protects eyes.
body: Children who spend more time outdoors are less likely to become short-sighted. Daylight helps. Aim for about two hours outside every day.
caption:
More and more children need glasses — and screens aren't the only reason. Time indoors is a big one.

Short-sightedness (myopia) is rising fast among children worldwide, including in India.

Studies show that kids who spend more time outdoors are less likely to develop myopia. Bright daylight seems to slow how the eye grows out of shape.

How to help your child:
→ Aim for about 2 hours outdoors a day, in total
→ Play, walk or cycle outside after school
→ Follow the 20-20-20 rule on screens
→ Get an eye check if they squint or sit close to the TV

It's good for adults' eyes and mood too.
